text: We close chapter four by coming back to a question lesson 11 first raised. Exactly what price does a simulated trade fill at, and could that fill have actually happened? Everything else can be modeled correctly and a backtest can still be unrealistic if this one assumption is physically impossible.

The guard has always been: a decision from bar N can only be acted on starting bar N plus one. But which price on that next bar? Filling at that next bar's close smuggles in a full extra day of movement you couldn't have captured. The realistic default for daily data is the next bar's open — the first price actually quoted once your signal is known.

Order type changes what a realistic fill even means. A market order fills at that next reference price plus slippage and impact. A limit order only fills if the market actually traded through your limit — you check the bar's low against the limit price, you don't just assume it filled because the signal said buy. Conflating these is testing a strategy that doesn't exist.

Before trusting any backtest, run this checklist. Name the exact fill price — never "the signal price." Check it's achievable for the order type you modeled. Confirm slippage and impact are layered in somewhere, not silently assumed away. And ask whether this fill logic would survive running live, bar by bar, with no knowledge of the future — the same look-ahead test from lesson 18, now aimed at execution.

Applying all five checks from this chapter — costs, impact, bias, overfitting, fills — typically makes a strategy's backtested performance worse, often a lot worse. That's not a flaw in the method; a strategy that survives all five intact is one actually worth taking seriously. Next, chapter five: lesson 21 covers returns, the Sharpe ratio, and the Sortino ratio — how to measure what survives this honestly.
